overview.summary: canary_server runs a command server for a workspace. Start it once on the machine that should do the work; send canary commands to it from anywhere the workspace is visible. Requests run one at a time, each as a child `canary` process, exactly as the command would run locally. Communication is through files in .canary/var/server/ (no sockets).
overview.start: canary server start   (blocks and logs to the terminal; background it with the shell, e.g. `nohup canary server start > server.log 2>&1 &`)
overview.submit: canary --connect=WHERE COMMAND ARGS   (run, exec, collect, select, hpc run): queues it and returns the request id; WHERE starts the workspace search ('.' = here)
overview.agents: canary server post '{"command": "run", "args": [...]}' prints {"id": ...}; then canary server get/wait/cancel ID

commands.start: Run the server for the current workspace in the foreground, printing each request and its output on the terminal. A second server for the same workspace is refused.
commands.stop: Ask the server to stop (works from any machine); interrupts the running request, keeps queued ones.
commands.status: Server alive?, the running request, the queue. --json for machine-readable output. Exit code 0 if alive.
commands.--connect: Global option --connect=WHERE: queue the command on the server of the workspace found from WHERE (a path inside/above the workspace or a file:// URL; '.' = here), print the request id, return at once. Unlike -C it keeps the caller's working directory, so relative paths mean what they mean where typed. The server prints the output on its terminal and keeps it with the request; follow with canary server wait ID. The server subcommands accept --connect too.
commands.post: Submit a request: JSON text (starts with {), a file holding it, or - for stdin; print {"id": ...}; --wait to follow.
commands.get: A request's record as JSON: command, args, state, position, returncode, times, stdout/stderr paths. --output prints the output.
commands.wait: Follow a request until it finishes and exit with its code; --quiet hides the output; Ctrl-C cancels the request.
commands.cancel: Cancel a queued request or interrupt a running one.

fields.command: run | exec | collect | select | hpc (hpc only with args[0] == 'run')
fields.args: Arguments after the command (list of strings).
fields.options: Global options before the command, e.g. ["-p", "myplugin"].
fields.cwd: Working directory, relative to the workspace anchor (dir holding .canary) or absolute; default '.' (the anchor). --connect records the caller's directory relative to the anchor.
fields.env: Variables to set on top of the server's environment (object of strings). Default: none. Only canary server post can set it.

files..canary/var/server/server.json: pid, host, started, heartbeat (every 2 s; dead after 10 s), version

behavior.ordering: Requests run one at a time, in arrival order; each gets the whole resource pool.
behavior.reads: status, query, log, info never go through the server; read the workspace directly.
behavior.protected: canary rm and canary run -w are refused while a server runs for the workspace; if the workspace disappears the server exits.
behavior.recovery: On restart, a request the dead server was running is marked failed; claimed-but-unstarted requests are requeued.
behavior.environment: Requests run in the server's environment as of `canary server start` (modules, PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, ...). Nothing from the client's environment is carried; load modules before starting the server, or post an explicit env.
behavior.working_directory: The request records the caller's directory (after -C) relative to the workspace anchor; the server runs the command in that directory under its own anchor and sets PWD to it. Path arguments are passed as typed, so relative paths keep their meaning even when the server's machine mounts the share elsewhere (/projects here, /gpfs/... there). Search paths (PATH, ...) come from the server's environment.
behavior.workspace_targeting: The command always works on the server's workspace (the server passes --canary-dir), and its arguments are parsed by the server, not the client: `canary --connect=WHERE run --only=failed` and `run JOBID` act on the server's workspace from any directory.

limitations: Fixed environment: changing modules means restarting the server; no --env option yet (use post's env).
One request at a time: hpc run holds the server while its batches wait on the scheduler.
Requires a shared filesystem; paths must mean the same thing on the server's machine.
Access control is the workspace directory's permissions.
No live status table: output is streamed as text.
In-process _canary.api.run.run does not go through the server.
